tn.quote: Magar Kaike reveals a number of typological features in the domain of phonology, morphology and syntax (Regmi, 2013). They are briefly presented as follows: 1.7.1 Phonological features (a) It has 32 consonant, six oral, three nasal vowels and six diphthongs. (b) The vowel length is not distinctive in Magar Kaike. (c) The maximum syllable structure: (C) (G) V (X), X, a consonant or a vowel. (d) There are six tones, three in low register and three in high register. (e) The stress is not distinctive in Magar Kaike but intonation is distinctive.

3912.tone: Terraced-level tone language, H vs. L, mora = TBU (p. 187, p. 364), with downdrift, downstep, H raising, floating L, OCP-style H-insertion between two L domains, tone spread, HLH leveling, boundary tones for illocutionary force (abstract). Low tonal density: 'closer to Japanese and Swedish than to Eton' (p. 350), but the author declines the pitch-accent label (fn. 1 cites Hyman 2009) and states that, unlike Swedish/Japanese, tonal oppositions 'are not restricted to one culminative syllable within a prosodic word' (p. 23). Word stress: the only Kakabe-referring statement is the p. 187 juxtaposition 'foot structure can be present in languages without phonetic stress. Kakabe is a language with moraic trochees'; every other 'stress' token in the thesis concerns French/Pular source words of loans (§5.5.5, pp. 402-405), the Pirahã/Russian/English onset-sensitivity analogy for H-separator alignment (§5.5.6.1, p. 409), or intonation theory (Ch. 6). The weight- and onset-sensitive foot parsing of L-toned trisyllables (heavy CVV/CVN closes a foot; otherwise the foot boundary precedes the stronger onset, rule 5.102, p. 408) governs where the separating H tone lands, which a compiler could mistake for a QS stress rule; it is a tone-alignment rule.

tn.quote: As for the basic oppositions, the tonal system of Kakabe is characterized by a three-way contrast: H vs. L vs. Ø. Underlyingly every tone bearing unit is assigned H, L or no tone at all (Ø). But at the end of the tonal derivation every tone bearing unit is linked either to H or L tone. Thus, the tree-way opposition at the lexical level gives a two-way opposition at the end of the phonological derivation ... [p. 364] In Kakabe the tone bearing unit (TBU henceforth) is the mora: ... mono-moraic syllables can have only one tone, but bi-moraic syllables can have two tones.

3920.dq: Über die Akzentuierung der kamassischen Wörter schreibt Donner: ... »Der Hauptakzent ruht gewöhnlich auf der ersten Silbe des Wortes. In zweisilbigen Wörtern ist er in der Hinsicht frei, dass er entweder auf die erste oder die zweite Silbe fällt. Wenn ein solches Wort einzeln ausgesprochen wird, fällt der Akzent sehr oft auf die zweite Silbe, besonders in tatarischen Lehnwörtern.«
3920.heavy: Joki/Donner: a long vowel or a diphthong in the second syllable ('Wenn der vokal der zweiten silbe lang ist, oder an dieser stelle ein diphthong steht, hat die zweite silbe den hauptakzent'). Klumpp 2016 (secondary, restating KW 126-127): heavy = closed syllable or long vowel; light = open with short or reduced vowel.
3920.dflt: first syllable ('Der Hauptakzent ruht gewöhnlich auf der ersten Silbe des Wortes')
3920.prule: Main (expiratory) accent usually on the first syllable of the word; if the second syllable contains a long vowel or a diphthong the main accent (often) moves to that second syllable; under Tatar influence the accent can instead fall on the last syllable. Klumpp 2016 restates the weight rule as: light first syllable (open, short or reduced vowel) + a following heavy syllable (closed, long vowel) -> accent moves to the heavy syllable (su.ra·r.ga, a.mo·r.zit.tǝ).
3920.srule: Donner (field notes 1912-14, quoted by Joki 1944 § 12): in words of three or more syllables with the main accent on the first syllable, a secondary accent (Nebenakzent) falls on the third syllable — stated as occasional in his Anleitung ('bisweilen, nicht aber regelmässig') and as the pattern of polysyllables in his grammatical notes; nothing is said about longer words. Joki adds that Donner's unexplained colon notation (word-final in his examples) probably marks this secondary accent.

3921.prule: No rule is stated anywhere in list 27; the only statement is the marking convention (note h: 'Syllables which are underlined carry the stress'). Re-read on (pp. 90-93, whole pages plus 4-5x crops of every disputed item): the underline sits on the penultimate syllable of the unsuffixed word in the large majority of marked polysyllables of 2-5 syllables (Patan, Oeroe, Polon, Tarina, Talapesi, Tahola, Alamana, Kamatian, Malapat, Masele, Malona, Mahina, Tamata, Sarampa, Atarea, Panikoe-nikoe, Ma'amalekoe, and the Malay loans Kapitan, Agama, Sembahjang, Naraka, Berdosa on p. 93), open and closed penults alike (Pa-tan, Ha-nal, Pe-len, Sa-ram-pa, Kas-ta). In words ending in -i/-e (which note i calls frequent suffixes) and in -ni/-re the mark usually sits one syllable further left, i.e. on the penult of the presumed root (ka-MA-ta-i, HA-toe-i (45), HOE-wa-i, HI-roe-i, LA-le-i, i-SI-sa-i, man-TE-roe-ni, HI-ra-i, HOE-ta-i, A-toe-i, A-na-i, RA-oe-i, ta-OE-roe-i, I-si-ni, pa-LA-roe-e, ma-ni-KE-roe-re, ma'a-MI-na-'e, ma'a-MOE-ri-'e), but not always: 105 ha-TOE-i carries the mark on the whole-word penult (198 is NA-wa-i, on the root penult). A handful of unsuffixed-looking words carry the mark on the antepenult (73 TA-i-a, 83 TI-ri-a, 118 OE-ra-ta, 185 MA-ta-ri, 299 ma-la-MA-i-te, 459 sa-LE-i-ne; all six confirmed at 5x zoom; the last two would be penult only if ai/ei counted as one syllable, which notes d and e deny). 3922.heavy: Not stated for Kamayo. For Bisayan dialects (the system Kamayo is said to preserve): 'In all Bs dialects studied, a closed penult is stressed. Thus, stress is predictable from the shape of the form' (Zorc 1977 sec. 8.10.2); an accented open penult is realised long ('The vowel in an accented, non-final, open syllable is long and stressed; the vowel in an unaccented or closed syllable is short', Zorc 1978: 72, Group A description).
3922.prule: Lexically contrastive (phonemic) word accent of the Proto-Central-Philippine / Bisayan type, which Kamayo 'generally preserves': accent falls on the penult or on the ultima per lexeme (an accented open penult is long and stressed), e.g. the PBS minimal pair punuq 'tree trunk' (penult) vs punuq 'full' (ultima); the position is not computable from syllable count. Kamayo is listed among the 'Philippine accent-preserving languages' in Zorc 1978 sec. 2.4 (Kamayo puruq 'island', ba:gaq 'lungs') and, in Zorc 1993: 18, among the languages from which examples of 'contrastive word accent' could be drawn. Within that inherited system a closed (CVC) penult is regularly stressed ('In all Bs dialects studied, a closed penult is stressed. Thus, stress is predictable from the shape of the form', Zorc 1977 sec. 8.10.2, p. 218) — stated for the Bisayan dialects and only implied for Kamayo via fn. 70 'preserves the PCP accent patterns'. Kamayo additionally has a phonemic long-vs-short contrast on FINAL vowels from compensatory lengthening after loss of *-l (Zorc 1977: 210-211; Zorc 1978: 71 Table 1 Group C, Kamayo qabo 'ashes' / qabo: 'smoke' < pre-Kam *qabal), a position inherited length never occupies; Zorc 1993 Table 2 class (C) restates this ('Length contrasts in the ultima, resulting from compensation for the loss of a consonant: Tausug, Butuanon, Kamayo, Cebuano').

3923.dq: não havendo acento na última sílaba, o vocábulo é paroxítono: kóbéni, não kóbéní.
3923.dloc: Grahl 2009, §3.3.1, pp. 59-60; footnote 2 attributes the key to 'Guérios, Mansur. Estudos sobre a Língua Kamakã. 1945, Empresa Gráfica paranaense Ltda.'; item 1 opens at the foot of p. 59 and continues on p. 60; p. 60 reads ó [ɔ], é [ɛ] where shows [O], [E].
3923.prule: No stress rule is stated in any reachable source. The only stress-bearing text is Guérios' (1945) key for reading the diacritics of his Kamakã wordlist (collected in February 1944), carried in Grahl 2009: the last accent mark in a word marks the tonic (a final acute or an added apostrophe = oxytone: kupã’, kópá’, kitxiãkü’); a word with no accent on its final syllable is paroxytone (kóbéni). This is a transcription convention, not a phonological statement: it implies that the marked tonic falls on the final or the penultimate syllable, item by item, but says nothing about whether the position is predictable (by weight, morphology or otherwise) or contrastive, and Guérios draws no generalisation from the marks himself (his vocabulary, pp. 298-304 of the 1945 original, carries them item by item; Grahl's Anexo B facsimile of it is illegible). Guérios' own caveat that the same word was recorded 'ora com um acento, ora com outro, e ora sem nada' (p. 05, quoted Grahl p. 62) further limits what the marks show. Translation of the quote: '1. The last accent is the tonic one: kupã, kópá, i.e. kupã’, kópá’. The others refer to vowel quality, as in Portuguese: ã nasal; à open, non-final; á open and final; ó [ɔ], é [ɛ] open; ô [o], ê [e] close. If there is no accent on the last syllable, the word is paroxytone: kóbéni, not kóbéní. Sometimes a is also open, non-final, and was written á. 2. Sometimes an acute was placed after the last, already accented, vowel; this is to indicate the tonic: kitxiãkü’.'
3923.srule: Not mentioned in Grahl 2009, §3.3 'Fonologia', pp. 58-68 (which reproduces Guérios 1945's pronunciation key, pp. 59-60: one tonic per word, marked item by item; no word on secondary stress).

3934.prule: Sources conflict on whether Karata has word stress at all. (a) The Russian descriptive tradition (Magomedbekova 1971 grammar and Magomedova & Khalidova 2001 dictionary as carried by Pasquereau, stress marked on every headword; first-hand in Dalgatov 2015/2017 for the Siwukh subdialect and Gadzhieva 2007 for the Tukita dialect): stress is weak, dynamic and mobile ('слабое динамическое, подвижное'), lexically and grammatically contrastive, with only tendencies for position - in disyllables mostly initial when the final syllable is open and on the second syllable when it is closed; second syllable in plural and oblique-stem forms of disyllabic nouns; in 3-5-syllable words 'разноместное' (free, 'особо не фиксированное'); Tukita infinitives stressed on the suffix -еду; Karata-proper nouns derived from masdars by shifting stress from 1st to 2nd syllable (Pakhrudinova 2004). Taken alone this would be lexical. (b) The most recent first-hand description of Karata village (Pasquereau, accepted HSK chapter): he and colleagues have not perceived a consistent stress pattern, the reported minimal pairs did not verify, stress may not be a salient or contrastive feature, possibly a Bagvalal-like clear/weak/no-stress three-way split; stress left unmarked and the question left open (neither lexical nor no word stress asserted). No fixed-position rule is stated by any source.

undet.detail: Lexical (free, mobile, weakly realised dynamic stress with an occasional contrastive/grammatical function), hedged. Evidence: stress position not fixed by count - 'подвижное', 'разноместное, особо не фиксированное' in 3-5-syllable words, 'может падать на разные слоги' in di-/trisyllables (Dalgatov 2015, 2017 Siwukh; Gadzhieva 2007 Tukita); minimal/near-minimal pairs by stress position…

3934.cfw: Magomedbekova's 1971 grammar, the Magomedova and Khalidova 2001 dictionary (stress marked on every headword, minimal pairs on p. 444), Pakhrudinova 2004, Gadzhieva 2007 for Tukita and Dalgatov 2015 and 2017 for Siwukh all describe Karata stress as weak, dynamic and mobile with an occasional contrastive function, whereas Pasquereau 2025, the most recent fieldworker, has not perceived a consistent stress pattern and leaves the existence of a stress system open, so the type of system is genuinely questioned but the weight of first-hand description favours weak mobile stress.

3935.dq: Structure de langue: traits remarquables: consonnes afriquées vibrantes rétroflexes; système tonal (quatre registres). (The statement concerns the language's tone system as a whole; no word- or phrase-level prominence is described.)
3935.dloc: LLACAN Fer page, section 'Structure de langue' (single-screen page); Boyeldieu & Nougayrol 2008 HAL MS pp.6-7 (incl. HAL cover).
3935.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Fer/Kara is characterised as a register-tone language with four contrastive tone levels (high, mid, low, extra-low 'infra-bas'); tone is lexical (nominal tone schemes; verbs carry two alternating tone schemes tied to lexical class). Neither reachable source mentions stress or accent at all.

3935.idn: Fer (« Kara »), autonym fɛ́r, région de Birao, nord de la RCA (Central African Republic); c. 4,000 speakers
3935.tone: Sources say nothing about stress or accent (a full-text search for accent|stress|intensit|syllabe intense|proéminence over all ten saved Boyeldieu texts and the LLACAN page: no hits). They establish a four-register lexical tone system for Fer ('système tonal (quatre registres)'; the fourth, extra-low level is a late, limited development shared with Yulu and Gula Koto). No source explicitly denies word stress, so the verdict rests on tone being the only word-prosodic property described.

tn.quote: 1.13 Le fer utilise à des fins distinctives la hauteur ou la modulation mélodiques qui contribuent ainsi à la définition d'une unité significative ... tonal fonctionne sur la base de quatre registres (haut, moyen, bas et infra-bas) qui fondent l'identité de plusieurs unités tonales pertinentes, simples ou modulées (pour les monosyllabes), uniformes ou contrastées (pour les dissyllabes) ... la pertinence semble bien se situer non pas au niveau du ton syllabique, mais à celui du schème tonal qui caractérise l'ensemble d'une unité significative
tn.translation: 1.13 Fer uses melodic pitch height or modulation distinctively; they contribute to defining a meaningful unit ... [the] tonal [system] works on the basis of four registers (high, mid, low and extra-low) which underlie several relevant tonal units, simple or modulated (for monosyllables), uniform or contrasting (for disyllables) ... the relevance seems to lie not at the level of the syllabic tone but at that of the tonal scheme characterising the whole meaningful unit
